title: Hospitality without grumbling (1 Peter 4:7–11)
hook: love covers a multitude of sins; use every gift for others
tomorrow: how do you throw a worry that won't let go of you?

segments.voice: A reason for hope, given to whoever asks, with gentleness and respect. The question came at the table. Today the table itself gets crowded.

A casserole on the porch, foil on top, still warm. Then another. Then the doorbell, again, and a coat to hang, and a chair to find, and somewhere in the kitchen a low mutter starts. So how do you open your door without the sigh? 1 Peter names that exact moment: "Use hospitality one to another without grudging." Not only open the door. Open it without the grumble. And the letter's way there begins with a strange sense of time.
screen: `A CASSEROLE ON THE PORCH.` → `THE MUTTER IN THE KITCHEN.` → `WITHOUT GRUDGING.`

segments.voice: It opens with urgency: "the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer." You'd expect the next line to be about the sky. It's about the people across the table. "And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins." Charity is the King James word for love. Some readers picture a blanket: the faults are still there, but love stops pulling the blanket back to look at them. The line echoes an older proverb: "love covereth all sins." Then the welcome, without grudging. Then the reason the grumble can go: "As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God." A steward looks after what belongs to someone else. The house, the soup, the knack for listening or fixing a sink: none of it started as yours to guard. And here's the detail to tell a friend: a welcome often speaks before anyone does. The smell of bread in the oven, coffee on, soup on the stove. A house can say come in, there's enough, before the door is even open. That's hospitality without grumbling, in a smell.
screen: `THE END IS NEAR: SO, THE TABLE.` · `CHARITY SHALL COVER.` · `STEWARDS, NOT OWNERS.` · `A WELCOME YOU CAN SMELL.` · then, large: `LOVE COVERS.`

segments.voice: Find something with a scent nearby: tea, coffee, an orange peel, bread, even a bar of soap. Breathe it in slowly, a few times, and notice how a smell says welcome before anyone speaks. On each breath out, let a little of the grumble go with it.
Hospitality without grumbling. First Peter, chapter four: welcome one another without grudging, and use every gift as a steward, for others.
Pocket this one: love covers, a blanket over the people at your table, not a spotlight. Rest easy.

options: 1 Peter: hospitality without grudging. The house is yours to steward, not guard. Say hi, then go study.

chat.meaning: 1 Peter asks for hospitality without grudging, and calls gifts things we steward for others. A real welcome can still leave room for a chem test.

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe; rewritten 2026-10-15 in recipe v3. Title, word, carry and sources kept. 1 Peter 4:11 (speak as the oracles of God, serve as of the ability God giveth) was cut from the voice for length; it stays cited.
The index title says 'grumbling'; the KJV says 'grudging'. The lesson quotes the KJV and glosses it.
'Some readers picture a blanket' marks the image as one reading of 1 Peter 4:8; others take 'cover' as forgiveness or as love covering one's own sins. Please check.
The link to Proverbs 10:12 is the standard cross-reference; 1 Peter does not name it. The lesson says the line 'echoes' it.
'A welcome often speaks before anyone does' (the smell of bread, coffee, soup) is the writer's sense picture, not a claim from the text.
